components.name: tool-call
components.title: Tool call
components.purpose: A summary of one tool call outside a transcript: the tool, its target, how it ended and how long it took, with the arguments and output behind disclosures.
whenToUse: In an activity view or a run's detail view, to show one tool call on its own or a short list of them.
When the reader needs the outcome of a call first and its arguments and output only on request.
whenNotToUse: For a tool call as a row of a transcript. Use a message of the tool-call kind, with a tool-result message after it.
For a call that still waits for the reader's answer. Use an approval, which carries Allow and Decline.
For a one-line record of what an agent did, among other events. Use an activity feed entry.

variants.name: succeeded
variants.use: The call returned without an error. The status reads Succeeded beside a check icon.

variants.name: failed
variants.use: The call ran and returned an error. The status reads Failed beside an alert icon, and gw-tool-call__note says what failed.

variants.name: denied
variants.use: The call was refused by the reader or by a permission rule and did not run. The status reads Denied beside a ban icon, and gw-tool-call__note says what was not run and why.

accessibility: Use an article with aria-labelledby pointing at gw-tool-call__title, a heading at the level the view needs. The title holds the tool name and then the target, both as text.
Several calls are li elements of a ul or ol, one article in each.
gw-tool-call__status always holds the status as a word: Running, Succeeded, Failed or Denied. The stylesheet draws the icon from the variant class, so the status is never colour alone.

While the call runs, set aria-busy="true" on the article and leave the variant class off. When it ends, remove aria-busy, add the variant class and change the word. Announce the change from a role="status" element in the view when the reader is waiting on it.
Write the duration with its unit, such as 2.4 s or 48 s so far. A duration that ticks is not in a live region.

Arguments and output each go in a native details element whose summary says what is inside and how long it is, such as Output, 6 lines. They start closed. Enter and Space open and close a summary, and its pointer target is 44px tall.
Write arguments and output as text, never as markup, and write out characters that cannot be seen. gw-tool-call__code wraps and never scrolls sideways.
It holds no action. The component needs no script: the app sets aria-busy, the variant class and the text.

examples.reason: The tool and its target can be read at a glance, the status is a word beside an icon, and the arguments and output stay one press away behind summaries that say what they hold.

components.name: tooltip
components.title: Tooltip
components.purpose: A line of supplementary text for a control that already has a visible label or an accessible name.
whenToUse: To add a detail to a labelled control: what exactly it will do, or its keyboard shortcut.
To show the name of an icon button to a sighted reader, when the button also carries that name for assistive technology.
whenNotToUse: As the only label of a control. Give the control a visible label or gw-visually-hidden text.
For anything the reader needs in order to act, such as why a button is unavailable or what a field accepts. Write it in the view, for example in the field's description.
For content with a link, a button or more than a sentence. Use a popover.
For an error. Use the field's error or an alert.

variants.name: above
variants.use: The default, with no modifier class. The text sits above the control, from its leading edge.

variants.name: below
variants.use: A control at the top of the screen, such as an action in the app header.

variants.name: end
variants.use: A control at the trailing edge of the view. The text lines up with the control's trailing edge and grows towards the start. It combines with gw-tooltip--below.

accessibility: Wrap the control in a span with the class gw-tooltip, and put the text straight after the control in a span with gw-tooltip__content, role="tooltip" and an id.
The control keeps its own name. Point its aria-describedby at the text, so a screen reader reads the text after the name.
The text holds words only: no link, no button, and nothing the reader cannot find elsewhere.
With that markup alone the tooltip opens on hover and on keyboard focus with no script, and stays open while the pointer is on the text. It closes when the pointer and the focus leave.

Add popover="hint" to the text and interestfor with the text's id to the control. A browser with interest invokers then also opens it on a long press on a touch screen, closes it on Escape, and draws it in the top layer where no container clips it. Other browsers ignore both attributes.

On a touch screen without interest invokers, a tap shows the tooltip only where the browser moves focus to a tapped button. iOS Safari does not. To cover it, the app listens for a long press on the control and calls showPopover({ source: control }) on the text, then hidePopover() on the next press anywhere. The text needs the popover attribute for that.

Without the popover attribute the text is clipped by an ancestor that hides its overflow. Use gw-tooltip--below under the top edge of the screen and gw-tooltip--end at the trailing edge, so the text stays on the screen.

components.name: undo-toast
components.title: Undo toast
components.purpose: A toast for an action that can be taken back: it says what happened, offers Undo and shows how long Undo stays.
whenToUse: After an action the app carries out at once and can fully reverse, such as archiving a task or removing runs from a board.
In place of a question before a reversible action. Acting and offering Undo is faster than asking first.
whenNotToUse: After an action the app cannot fully reverse, such as deleting a workspace from disk. Ask first with the confirm dialog.
For a message with nothing to take back. Use a toast.
When Undo is the only way back. The reader must also be able to restore the thing elsewhere, such as from an Archived list.

variants.name: words
variants.use: The default. gw-undo-toast__countdown under the message says how many seconds are left.

variants.name: progress
variants.use: A native progress element with gw-undo-toast__progress after the button, as well as the words. Its max is the seconds Undo stays and its value the seconds left.

accessibility: Use the toast markup inside the page's gw-toast__region, with gw-toast, gw-toast--success and gw-undo-toast on the toast element. The message says what happened and to what: Task 41 archived.

Undo is the toast's one action, a button with gw-button gw-button--small gw-toast__action. The toast never takes focus, so also give the reader a way back that does not expire, such as a Restore button in the Archived list.
The app keeps the toast for at least 10 seconds, and pauses its timer while the pointer is over the toast or focus is inside it. When the time runs out the app removes the toast.

Once a second the app writes the seconds left into gw-undo-toast__countdown, and sets the value attribute of the progress element when there is one. Both carry aria-hidden="true", so a screen reader is not interrupted every second. A gw-visually-hidden sentence in the message says the whole time once: You have 10 seconds to undo.

When Undo is pressed, set aria-busy="true" on it, change its label to say what is happening, such as Restoring task, and remove the countdown. Then replace the toast with a plain toast that says the thing is back.
If the undo fails, replace the toast with a gw-toast--danger one that says the thing is still archived and what to do, with Undo again as its action.

components.name: usage-meter
components.title: Usage meter
components.purpose: How much of a limit is used, on a native meter, with the figures and the state written in words.
whenToUse: For use against a known limit: tokens for a run, runs in a month, storage for worktrees.
With the row variant in a cell of a usage table or in a list row, where the row already names what is measured.
whenNotToUse: For the progress of a task towards being done. Use a progress element, or a spinner when the length is not known.
When there is no limit. Write the number as text, or use a stat.
For a number with a comparison and no limit. Use the stat.
For a status. Use a badge.

variants.name: default
variants.use: The label and the state on one line, the bar under them, the figures under the bar.

variants.name: row
variants.use: The bar, the figures and the state on one line, with no label of its own. The meter takes an aria-label that names what the row measures.

accessibility: Use a meter element with the class gw-usage-meter__bar. Set min, max and value from the data, and put the figures as text inside it for a browser that cannot draw it.
Name the meter: aria-labelledby pointing at gw-usage-meter__label, or aria-label in the row variant.
Always write the figures with their unit in gw-usage-meter__figures, such as 18,420 of 50,000 tokens. The bar never stands alone.

The tone comes from the meter's own thresholds, so no class follows the value. Set optimum="0", low to the value where the warning starts and high to the value where the limit is reached or nearly so. The bar is neutral up to low, takes the warning tone between low and high, and the danger tone above high.
Say the same state in words in gw-usage-meter__state, and choose the words by the same thresholds: Within the limit, Near the limit, Over the limit. Colour is never the only signal.
A value above max draws a full bar. Write the real figures, such as 214 of 200 runs, and say what happens next.
With nothing used, keep the meter at 0 and say so. While the figures load, show a spinner in place of the meter. If they cannot be read, show an error message in its place, never an empty bar.
When the state changes while the reader watches, announce it from a role="status" element in the view. The meter is not focusable and needs no script beyond setting its attributes and text.
